sections.intro:
Céüse isn't a crag you stumble into — you earn it. A legendary 45-minute uphill approach serves as both warm-up and penance, rewarding you with what a lot of very opinionated climbers consider the finest limestone on the planet.

The 300-metre blue-gray cliff band is a technical masterclass: delicate crimps, perfect pockets, subtle sidepulls, and the occasional water-sculpted tufa that will humble anyone who thinks "technical" is a synonym for "easy."

Seven days working classic testpieces beneath lavender-scented hills, evenings spent with local wine, cheese, and baguettes back at camp — because France insists on doing suffering beautifully.

paragraphs.text: Perched high above the lavender fields of Provence, Céüse's 300-metre limestone band curves in a perfect arc — home to some of the most aesthetic lines ever bolted, including the legendary Biographie.

Seven days climbing above a river you'll actually want to swim in, evenings spent on aligot and local wine in villages that cling improbably to the canyon walls.

Labské Údolí — the "Czech Yosemite," or Bohemian Switzerland if you're feeling fancy — is the opening chapter of our 8-week Rock & Road tour across Europe. It's also the one that humbles egos fastest.

Forget bolts. Czech sandstone runs on knotted slings, gear that looks sketchier than it is, and an ethical code older than your grandparents. Smearing beats edging, nerve beats power, and climbers here were "head-pointing" routes before it had a name.

Seven days of towering spires by day, goulash and pilsner in centuries-old pubs by night. This isn't a soft intro to European rock — it's a portal into climbing's stubborn, soulful past.

paragraphs.text: Also known as Bohemian Switzerland, Labské Údolí is a national park of sandstone towers rising out of misty river gorges along the Elbe. It's less a crag, more a fairytale that happens to have quickdraws in it.
The climbing style is unlike anywhere else in Europe — no bolts, no shortcuts, and protection rules strict enough to make you a sharper, calmer climber whether you like it or not.

sections.heading: Where Cobblestones Defy Gravity
sections.intro:
Margalef's conglomerate rock is unlike anything else on the tour — a matrix of rounded cobbles set in cement-like stone, studded across walls that genuinely look like they shouldn't hold weight. They do. Mostly.

This is pocket pulling in its most extreme form: shallow monos that barely accept a fingertip, deep three-finger holes that count as a rest. The deep red and orange walls rise from olive groves and pine forest, with the occasional hermitage wedged impossibly into the cliff.

Seven days climbing in a distinctly Catalan atmosphere — passionate, proud, and just as obsessed with the send as you are — evenings spent recovering by the reservoir and eating well in the village.

sections.heading: Where the Rock Hides Well
sections.intro:
Oltre Finale — literally "beyond Finale" — is the tour's best-kept secret. Tucked into the "Valley of the Rock" past the crowds of Finale Ligure proper, this is where 2,000+ routes of compact limestone sit quietly waiting for people willing to drive a little further.

Expect a bit of everything: technical crimps, perfect pockets, the occasional tufa, and faces ranging from delicate slabs to genuinely rude overhangs. Creative movement isn't optional here — it's the whole curriculum.

Seven days climbing sun-warmed limestone by day, cooling off in mountain streams and eating your way through Ligurian villages by night — where the espresso is strong and nobody's in a hurry.
